title: The ideal gas model
html:
Guiding question

How does the model of ideal gas behaviour help us to predict the behaviour of real gases?

Think of a car parked in the UAE desert. By mid-afternoon the air temperature can pass 45 °C and the road surface is far hotter; at night it can drop below 15 °C. The air sealed inside each tyre responds to every one of those changes, and so does the tyre pressure, the grip, the wear and the fuel economy. To predict what happens we need a model of how a gas behaves. This topic builds that model, tests it with the gas laws, and then asks when real gases stop obeying it.

CodeUnderstanding
S1.5.1An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
S1.5.2Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
S1.5.3The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
S1.5.4The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation pV = nRT and the combined gas law p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.
Key point · starterThe gas laws use moles, so warm up: 2 mol of O₂ contains 2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules, and because each molecule is diatomic it contains 2 × 1.20 × 10²⁴ = 2.41 × 10²⁴ O atoms.

S1.5.1 The ideal gas model

Gases are mostly empty space: water vapour takes up about 1600 times the volume of the same mass of liquid water. The ideal gas model is a simplified picture built on these assumptions:

  1. Gas particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion.
  2. The volume of the particles themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
  3. There are no intermolecular forces of attraction or repulsion between particles (so an ideal gas would never condense).
  4. All collisions, with each other and with the walls, are perfectly elastic: total kinetic energy is conserved.
  5. The average kinetic energy of the particles is directly proportional to the absolute (Kelvin) temperature.
Exam tip"State two assumptions of the ideal gas model" — the safest answers are negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces. These are also the two that break down for real gases, which sets up the next question.

Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container. Pressure = force ÷ area, SI unit the pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). 1 atm = 101.3 kPa. More frequent or harder collisions mean a higher pressure.

Which is not an assumption of the ideal gas model?

  1. Particles are in constant random motion
  2. Particles have negligible volume
  3. Particles attract each other weakly
  4. Collisions are perfectly elastic

An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces at all. Weak attractions are a property of real gases, which is why they can condense.

Why does gas pressure increase when more gas is pumped into a rigid container at constant temperature?

  1. The particles move faster
  2. The particles become larger
  3. There are more collisions with each unit area of wall per second
  4. The collisions become less elastic

Same T means the same average speed; more particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions with the walls, so a greater force per unit area.

Fill the gap: in an ideal gas, all collisions are perfectly elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved.

title: Real gases and deviations
html:
S1.5.2 Real gases and deviation from ideal behaviour

Real gas particles do have a volume and do attract each other. Under most everyday conditions these effects are small, but they matter at:

  • High pressure: the particles are squeezed close together, so their own volume becomes a significant fraction of the container volume. Only the space between particles can be compressed, so the real volume is larger than predicted. Particles are also close enough for attractions to act.
  • Low temperature: particles move slowly, so their kinetic energy is not much bigger than the energy of the intermolecular attractions. Particles "stick" briefly when they collide, hit the walls less often and less hard, and the pressure is lower than predicted. Eventually the gas condenses.
Key pointReal gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure: particles are far apart (own volume negligible) and moving fast (attractions negligible).

Which gases deviate most? Gases with stronger intermolecular forces and larger particles deviate more under comparable conditions (link to S2.2):

  • He and H₂ are closest to ideal: tiny particles and only weak London forces.
  • Polar molecules (HCl, SO₂) and especially hydrogen-bonded molecules (NH₃, H₂O) deviate much more.
  • Within a homologous series, larger molecules (more electrons, stronger London forces, bigger volume) deviate more: butane deviates more than methane.

A useful test is the compression factor pV/nRT, which equals exactly 1 for an ideal gas. Values below 1 mean attractions dominate; values above 1 (at very high pressure) mean particle volume dominates.

Common mistakeSaying a gas deviates at high pressure "because particles collide more". The answer must refer to particle volume no longer negligible and/or intermolecular forces no longer negligible, since these are the assumptions that fail.

Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?

  1. Low temperature, low pressure
  2. Low temperature, high pressure
  3. High temperature, high pressure
  4. High temperature, low pressure

High T: particles move fast, so attractions are negligible. Low p: particles are far apart, so their volume is negligible.

Under comparable conditions, which gas deviates most from ideal behaviour?

  1. He
  2. H₂
  3. CH₄
  4. NH₃

NH₃ molecules form hydrogen bonds, the strongest intermolecular forces here, so attractions reduce the pressure most below the ideal value.

Explain why a real gas has a lower pressure than predicted at low temperature. Write your answer, then reveal a model answer.

At low temperature the particles have low kinetic energy, so intermolecular attractions are no longer negligible compared with it. Particles are pulled towards each other (and away from the walls) as they approach the wall, so they hit the walls less often and with less force. The measured pressure is therefore lower than pV = nRT predicts.

title: Molar volume of a gas
html:
S1.5.3 Molar volume of an ideal gas

From Avogadro's law (S1.4.6), one mole of any ideal gas occupies the same volume at a given temperature and pressure.

n = V ÷ Vm     Vm = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa)
  • The value 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ and the STP conditions are in section 2 of the data booklet.
  • Older resources and past papers use 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ (at 101.3 kPa) or 24 dm³ mol⁻¹ (at "room temperature and pressure", about 298 K). Always use the value or conditions given in the question.
  • Molar volume changes with T and p, so at non-standard conditions use pV = nRT instead.
Worked example · gas produced in a reaction3.25 g of zinc reacts with excess sulfuric acid: Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g). Find the volume of H₂ at STP.
n(Zn) = 3.25 ÷ 65.38 = 0.0497 mol = n(H₂) (1 : 1)
V = 0.0497 × 22.7 = 1.13 dm³
Worked example · molar mass from gas density2.00 dm³ of a gas at STP has a mass of 2.47 g.
n = 2.00 ÷ 22.7 = 0.0881 mol; M = 2.47 ÷ 0.0881 = 28.0 g mol⁻¹ (could be N₂, CO or C₂H₄).

0.160 g of calcium carbide, CaC₂, reacts with excess water: CaC₂(s) + 2H₂O(l) → C₂H₂(g) + Ca(OH)₂(s). Calculate the volume of ethyne at STP in cm³.

M(CaC₂) = 40.08 + 2 × 12.01 = 64.10 g mol⁻¹. n = 0.160 ÷ 64.10 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol = n(C₂H₂) (1 : 1). V = 2.50 × 10⁻³ × 22.7 = 0.0567 dm³ = 56.7 cm³.

What amount of gas (mol) occupies 4.54 dm³ at STP?

n = V ÷ Vm = 4.54 ÷ 22.7 = 0.200 mol

Under what conditions would one mole of methane occupy the smallest volume?

  1. 273 K and 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa
  2. 273 K and 2.02 × 10⁵ Pa
  3. 546 K and 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa
  4. 546 K and 2.02 × 10⁵ Pa

V = nRT/p is smallest when T is low and p is high: 273 K and 2.02 × 10⁵ Pa.

Air bags inflate when sodium azide decomposes: 2NaN₃(s) → 2Na(s) + 3N₂(g). What amount of N₂ forms from 2.52 mol of NaN₃?

  1. 1.68 mol
  2. 2.52 mol
  3. 3.78 mol
  4. 7.56 mol

Ratio NaN₃ : N₂ = 2 : 3, so 2.52 × 3/2 = 3.78 mol N₂ (about 86 dm³ at STP).

title: The gas laws and the combined gas law
html:
S1.5.4 The gas laws

Four variables describe a gas sample: pressure p, volume V, absolute temperature T and amount n. To study two of them, hold the other two constant. Each law below was discovered experimentally, and each follows directly from the ideal gas model.

LawConstantRelationshipEquationGraph
Boyle's lawn, Tp inversely proportional to Vp₁V₁ = p₂V₂p against V: curve (hyperbola); p against 1/V: straight line through origin
Charles's lawn, pV directly proportional to T (K)V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂V against T(K): straight line through origin; in °C the line extrapolates to −273 °C
Gay-Lussac's (pressure) lawn, Vp directly proportional to T (K)p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂p against T(K): straight line through origin
Avogadro's lawp, TV directly proportional to nV₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂V against n: straight line through origin

Boyle's law

For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume varies inversely with pressure: pV = constant. A classroom demonstration: draw a face on a marshmallow, seal it in a syringe and pull the plunger out. The pressure around the marshmallow falls, the air trapped inside it expands, and the marshmallow swells; push the plunger in and it shrinks again.

Charles's law

For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, the volume is directly proportional to the Kelvin temperature: V/T = constant. Hot-air balloons, a familiar sight over the UAE desert, work this way: heating the air inside expands it at (roughly) constant pressure, so some air is pushed out of the opening, the balloon's contents become less dense than the surrounding air, and it rises. The pilot controls altitude by heating (rise) or letting the air cool (descend).

Gay-Lussac's (pressure) law

For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the pressure is directly proportional to the Kelvin temperature: p/T = constant. This is the tyre in the desert: the tyre's volume barely changes, so the pressure follows the temperature.

Avogadro's law

Particle explanations (needed for "explain" questions):

  • Boyle: halving the volume packs the same particles into half the space, so they hit each unit area of wall twice as often → pressure doubles.
  • Gay-Lussac: raising T increases the average kinetic energy, so particles hit the walls more often and with more force → pressure rises.
  • Charles: at constant pressure, faster particles push the walls (or piston) outwards until the collision rate per unit area falls back to its original value → volume increases.
Key point · always use kelvinThe proportionalities only work from absolute zero. T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 (273 is accepted). Doubling the temperature from 20 °C to 40 °C does not double the volume: 293 K → 313 K is only a 7% increase. A temperature change is the same size in K and °C.

A sealed container in a desert research facility starts at 3.0 atm. Its temperature is raised from 30 °C to 80 °C. Which law applies?

  1. Boyle's law
  2. Charles's law
  3. Gay-Lussac's (pressure) law
  4. Avogadro's law

The container is sealed and rigid, so n and V are fixed while T changes: that is the pressure law, p/T = constant. Boyle's law needs constant temperature, so it cannot be used when T changes.

For the container above, calculate the final pressure.

T₁ = 30 + 273 = 303 K; T₂ = 80 + 273 = 353 K. p₂ = p₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁ = 3.0 × 353 ÷ 303 = 3.5 atm.

A container holds 10.0 L of nitrogen containing 0.50 mol. Gas is added until there is 1.0 mol, at constant T and p. New volume?

V₂ = V₁ × n₂ ÷ n₁ = 10.0 × 1.0 ÷ 0.50 = 20.0 L. Industrial gas storage relies on this proportionality.

The combined gas law

p₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂V₂ ÷ T₂    (fixed amount of gas)

Any units of p and V may be used, as long as they are the same on both sides. T must be in kelvin.

Worked example · tyre pressure in the desertA tyre is inflated to 30 psi during the day at 50 °C. At night the temperature falls to 10 °C. Assuming the volume is constant, find the night-time pressure.
T₁ = 323 K, T₂ = 283 K
p₂ = p₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁ = 30 × 283 ÷ 323 = 26 psi
The tyre is under-inflated at night (more rolling resistance, more wear, poorer fuel economy), so pressures should be checked when tyres are cold. Tyres made for the Gulf region use heat-resistant rubber compounds for the same reason.
Worked example · hot-air balloonA balloon holds 2000 m³ of air at 45 °C. At altitude the temperature is 10 °C (constant p). V₂ = 2000 × 283 ÷ 318 = 1780 m³. Heating the air expands it, lowering its density, which is what makes the balloon rise.
Worked example · quick ratio reasoningA fixed mass of gas occupies 800 cm³. Its pressure and Kelvin temperature are both doubled. V₂ = 800 × (1/2) × 2 = 800 cm³ — no change.
If T (K) is doubled and p is quadrupled: V₂ = V₁ × 2 ÷ 4 = V₁/2.
Worked example · all three variables changeA fixed mass of gas at 20 °C has its pressure raised from 101 Pa to 303 Pa and its volume from 1 m³ to 6 m³. Find the final temperature.
T₂ = T₁ × (p₂V₂) ÷ (p₁V₁) = 293 × (303 × 6) ÷ (101 × 1) = 293 × 18 = 5274 K
Pressure ×3 and volume ×6 means pV ×18, so T must also rise 18-fold.
Exam tipMultiple-choice gas-law questions are fastest by ratio reasoning: V ∝ nT/p. Write down how each factor changes, multiply, and you have the answer without a calculator.

The temperature (in K) of 2.0 dm³ of an ideal gas is doubled and its pressure is increased by a factor of four. What is the final volume?

  1. 1.0 dm³
  2. 2.0 dm³
  3. 3.0 dm³
  4. 4.0 dm³

V ∝ T/p: × 2 ÷ 4 = × ½, so 2.0 → 1.0 dm³.

A cylinder of gas is at 40 kPa. Its volume and Kelvin temperature are both doubled. What is the new pressure?

  1. 10 kPa
  2. 20 kPa
  3. 40 kPa
  4. 80 kPa

p ∝ T/V: × 2 ÷ 2 = × 1, so the pressure stays at 40 kPa.

Which change would increase the volume of a fixed mass of gas?

  1. p doubled, T (K) doubled
  2. p halved, T halved
  3. p doubled, T halved
  4. p halved, T doubled

V ∝ T/p: A × 1, B × 1, C × ¼, D × 4. Only D increases the volume.

The temperature in kelvin of 1.0 dm³ of an ideal gas is doubled and its pressure is tripled. Final volume?

V₂ = 1.0 × 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67 dm³ (⅔ dm³).

A balloon contains 2000 m³ of air at 45 °C. At altitude the air cools to 10 °C at constant pressure. New volume?

V₂ = V₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁ = 2000 × 283 ÷ 318 = 1780 m³. Remember: convert both temperatures to kelvin first.
State and explain what happens to the pressure of a fixed mass of gas when its absolute temperature and volume are both doubled. Predict, then reveal.

The pressure stays the same. Doubling T doubles the average kinetic energy, so particles hit the walls harder and more often, which on its own would double p. Doubling V halves the number of particles per unit volume, which on its own would halve the collision frequency per unit area. The two effects cancel: p ∝ T/V = 2/2 = 1.

title: The ideal gas equation and molar mass of a gas
html:
The ideal gas equation

Combining all four laws gives one equation that links every variable. The constant of proportionality is the gas constant R.

pV = nRT     R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
QuantitySI unitCommon conversion
pPakPa × 1000 → Pa; 1 atm = 101 325 Pa
Vm³dm³ × 10⁻³ → m³; cm³ × 10⁻⁶ → m³
TK°C + 273.15
nmoln = m ÷ M
Key point · unit pairsEither use Pa with m³, or use kPa with dm³ — both give the correct n with R = 8.31, because the factors of 10³ and 10⁻³ cancel. Mixing them (kPa with m³, or Pa with dm³) gives an answer 10⁶ times too big or small, the single most common error in this topic.
Worked example · molar volume at STP from pV = nRTV = nRT ÷ p = (1 × 8.31 × 273.15) ÷ 100 000 = 0.0227 m³ = 22.7 dm³. At 101.3 kPa the same calculation gives 22.4 dm³, the older textbook value.

Calculate the volume in dm³ of 1.00 mol of an ideal gas at 0 °C and 101 kPa.

V = nRT ÷ p = (1.00 × 8.31 × 273) ÷ 101 000 = 0.0225 m³ = 22.5 dm³. This is the molar volume at these conditions: any ideal gas, one mole, same volume.

A student calculates n = pV/RT using p = 98 kPa and V = 472 cm³ converted to 4.72 × 10⁻⁴ m³, without converting p. How does the answer compare with the correct value?

  1. Correct
  2. 1000 times too small
  3. 1000 times too large
  4. 10⁶ times too large

Using kPa with m³ makes p 1000 times too small (98 instead of 98 000), so n is 1000 times too small. Pair Pa with m³, or kPa with dm³.

Determining the molar mass of a gas

Combining pV = nRT with n = m/M gives:

M = mRT ÷ pV
Worked example · a hydrocarbon0.688 g of a hydrocarbon occupies 472 cm³ at 98.0 kPa and 67 °C.
n = pV ÷ RT = (98 000 × 4.72 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (8.31 × 340) = 0.0164 mol
M = 0.688 ÷ 0.0164 = 42.0 g mol⁻¹ → C₃H₆ (propene, M = 42.09)
Follow-on: volume of O₂ (STP) to burn 0.21 g: C₃H₆ + 4.5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 3H₂O; n(C₃H₆) = 0.21 ÷ 42.09 = 0.00499 mol; n(O₂) = 0.0225 mol; V = 0.0225 × 22.7 = 0.51 dm³.
Worked example · vapour of a volatile liquid0.230 g of a liquid, when vaporised, occupies 0.0785 dm³ at 95 °C and 102 kPa. Its empirical formula is C₂H₄O.
n = (102 × 0.0785) ÷ (8.31 × 368) = 2.62 × 10⁻³ mol (kPa and dm³ used together)
M = 0.230 ÷ 2.62 × 10⁻³ = 87.8 g mol⁻¹
M(C₂H₄O) = 44.06, factor 2 → molecular formula C₄H₈O₂

A toxic gas is 53.8% N and 46.2% C by mass. At 273 K and 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.048 g occupies 462 cm³. Calculate its molar mass.

n = pV ÷ RT = (1.01 × 10⁵ × 4.62 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (8.31 × 273) = 0.0206 mol. M = 1.048 ÷ 0.0206 = 51.0 g mol⁻¹. Empirical formula: N 53.8 ÷ 14.01 = 3.84, C 46.2 ÷ 12.01 = 3.85 → CN (26.02); 51 ÷ 26 ≈ 2 → C₂N₂ (cyanogen, 52.04).
Worked example · combining pV = nRT with stoichiometry2.00 cm³ of ethanol burns completely: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). 2.500 dm³ CO₂ is collected at 101.3 kPa and 298 K.
n(CO₂) = (101.3 × 2.500) ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 0.102 mol
n(ethanol) = 0.102 ÷ 2 = 0.0511 mol → m = 0.0511 × 46.08 = 2.36 g
Density of ethanol = 2.36 ÷ 2.00 = 1.18 g cm⁻³ (the true value is 0.79 g cm⁻³: the numbers in this question are idealised, since 2.00 cm³ of real ethanol would give only about 1.7 dm³ of CO₂ — a good evaluation point).
Common mistakeMixing up which substance the moles belong to. pV = nRT gives n of the gas measured (here CO₂, 0.102 mol). Only after using the 1 : 2 ratio do you have n(ethanol) = 0.0511 mol. Labelling 0.05 mol as "n(CO₂)" is a slip that costs marks even if the final number is right.

Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at 273 K and 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa when 1.25 g of CaCO₃ reacts completely with hydrochloric acid. Answer in dm³.

CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. n(CaCO₃) = 1.25 ÷ 100.09 = 0.0125 mol = n(CO₂). V = nRT ÷ p = 0.0125 × 8.31 × 273 ÷ 1.01 × 10⁵ = 2.81 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 0.281 dm³.

Practical: the molar mass of the gas in a lighter

How can the ideal gas law find the Mr of the hydrocarbon in a disposable lighter? We need n (from p, V and T) and the mass of gas (from weighing the lighter before and after).

Practical · molar mass of butane from a lighter
  1. Record the room/water temperature and atmospheric pressure (barometer or weather app).
  2. Weigh the lighter.
  3. Fill a measuring cylinder with water and invert it in a trough of water with no air bubbles.
  4. Hold the lighter under the cylinder and release gas (do not strike it) until about 50–100 cm³ has been collected. Level the water inside and outside the cylinder so the gas is at atmospheric pressure, and read the volume.
  5. Dry the lighter thoroughly and reweigh it.
  6. Calculate n = pV/RT (Pa, m³, K), then M = mass lost ÷ n. Compare with M(C₄H₁₀) = 58.14 g mol⁻¹ and find the percentage error.
Sources of error: water left on the lighter (mass loss too small → M too low); some gas escaping or dissolving in water; the collected gas is saturated with water vapour, so p(butane) = p(atm) − p(water vapour) — ignoring this makes n too large and M too low; lighter gas is often a butane/propane/isobutane mixture. Safety: no naked flames, butane is extremely flammable.

Sample results: water temperature 21 °C, pressure 101.0 kPa, 100 cm³ of gas collected, lighter mass 15.36 g before and 15.12 g after. Calculate M of the gas.

T = 294 K; p = 101 000 Pa; V = 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³. n = pV ÷ RT = 10.1 ÷ (8.31 × 294) = 4.13 × 10⁻³ mol. Mass of gas = 0.24 g. M = 0.24 ÷ 4.13 × 10⁻³ = 58 g mol⁻¹ → consistent with butane, C₄H₁₀ (58.14). Percentage error ≈ 0.1%.
Linking to empirical formulas: a hydrocarbon contains 24 g of carbon and 5 g of hydrogen; its molar mass (from the lighter experiment) is 58 g mol⁻¹. Find the empirical and molecular formulas.

C 24 ÷ 12.01 = 2.00; H 5 ÷ 1.01 = 4.95 → 1 : 2.48 ≈ 2 : 5 → empirical formula C₂H₅ (M = 29.06). 58 ÷ 29.06 = 2 → molecular formula C₄H₁₀, butane. Alkanes fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and n = 4 gives 58.14.

Practical · investigating p against TA sealed flask of air in a water bath, connected to a pressure gauge, with a thermometer in the bath. Independent variable: temperature; dependent: pressure; controlled: volume and amount of gas. A graph of p against T(K) is a straight line through the origin. Sketched graphs show the shape of a relationship quickly; accurately plotted points allow gradients, intercepts (absolute zero) and uncertainty to be found.

Common exam pitfalls

  • Temperature left in °C in pV = nRT or the combined gas law.
  • Mismatched units (kPa with m³). Write the units next to every number before substituting.
  • Using 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ when the conditions are not STP.
  • Applying gas volumes to liquids: H₂O(l) has no "gas volume" in an Avogadro calculation.
  • Rounding n before calculating M, which can shift the final answer outside the mark-scheme range.
Linking questionsS2.2 — Under comparable conditions, why do some gases deviate more from ideal behaviour than others? R2.2 — Graphs can be sketched or plotted accurately; what are the advantages of each? Tool 1, Inquiry 2 — How can the ideal gas law be used to find the molar mass of a gas from experimental data?
